label: Afternoon edition
summary: Keanu, **polls are closing on Election Day** and the Senate call may take far longer than the House (NPR, Fox News). Final polls favor Democrats in several Republican-held Senate seats, but Fox ratings still list Texas, Maine and Michigan as toss-ups (NPR, CNN, Fox News). Pew has Trump's approval at 37% and Democrats lead the generic ballot by about 9 points (Washington Examiner, The Dispatch). On your ballot, **Prop 40 trailed at 46% to 52%**, and Props 41 or 42 can cancel it even if it passes, while the regional transit tax needs only a simple majority (KQED, CalMatters, SF Chronicle). The Justice Department says it will appeal the dismissal of its Alaska ballot suit (CNN, Fox News). The U.S. hit Iran's Qeshm Island in what officials call a defensive strike, and oil rose, with WTI at $96.74 (CNN, CNBC). A Russian bombing in Zaporizhzhia killed at least 33 (CNN, NPR). On Wall Street, the S&P 500 rose 0.36% and the Nasdaq 0.83%, but Apple fell 1.90% after a weak margin forecast (CNBC). Anthropic could start **IPO marketing the week of Nov. 9** (Bloomberg). NASA's Swift telescope should fall near **12:30 a.m. Pacific Wednesday** (NASA, Space.com).

alerts.text: Prop 40, Props 41 and 42, and the Bay Area transit tax are all being decided tonight, and close counts can take days.
NASA's Swift telescope is due to re-enter around 12:30 a.m. Pacific Wednesday, with a 1-in-2,100 risk of harm to anyone.
Anthropic could begin IPO marketing as soon as the week of Nov. 9.
Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17 after the close.

Oil rose after the reported U.S. strike on Qeshm, with WTI at $96.74 and the 10-year yield at 4.95% (CNBC, live data). **Bitcoin rose 1.33%** to $77,705 (live data).

stories.title: Polls close across the country with control of Congress undecided
stories.summary: Control of the House and Senate is at stake tonight, and NPR warns the Senate call could take much longer than the House.
story: Polls began closing at 6 p.m. Eastern Tuesday, with Kentucky's 6th and Indiana's 5th districts first, according to NPR's election-night guide. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot (Fox News, Axios). No results had been reported in the coverage found when this edition was written.

Republicans defend slim majorities in both chambers. Fox News says Republicans need 50 Senate seats to keep control, because Vice President JD Vance breaks ties. Democrats need a net gain of three House seats to flip that chamber (Washington Examiner). Early voting set records, with more than 54 million ballots cast, per the Associated Press as cited by Fox News.

NPR says House control could become clear sooner, while the Senate may take far longer, partly because two states use ranked-choice voting. Florida, which redrew its congressional map, is an early test. The Washington Examiner reports that White House aides project optimism publicly while sweating the result in private. Fox News reports Trump predicted a Republican hold.
facts: Polls open to close in stages from 6 p.m. Eastern, per NPR.
Kentucky's 6th and Indiana's 5th report first (NPR).
All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are up (Fox News).
Republicans need 50 Senate seats to hold control (Fox News).
Record early vote: more than 54 million ballots (AP via Fox News).
stories.next: Results start flowing after 6 p.m. Eastern. The Senate may not be called tonight.
stories.left: Democrats say record early turnout and Trump's low approval point to a correction, and they frame the vote as a referendum on prices and the Iran war. They argue the House is within reach and that a Democratic House would bring oversight of the White House. The risk they name is complacency, since Democrats' own image is weak.
stories.right: Republicans argue polls undercount their voters and that the Senate map is friendlier than surveys suggest. They point to strong Election Day turnout in Florida, Ohio and Texas and to Trump's final rally push in red states. A Senate hold, they say, would let the president still claim a win and keep confirming judges and nominees.

stories.title: Final polls put Democrats ahead in several Republican-held Senate seats, but ratings still call it a toss-up
stories.summary: Polls show Democrats leading in Texas, Maine, Ohio and Michigan, while Fox ratings keep several races toss-ups.
story: The final public polls favor Democrats in several races, according to coverage compiled by NPR, CNN and Fox News. A New York Times/Siena poll found Democrat James Talarico ahead of Republican Ken Paxton 50% to 43% in Texas, and Democrat Troy Jackson ahead of Republican Susan Collins 51% to 45% in Maine. In Michigan the same poll had Democrat Abdul El-Sayed ahead of Republican Mike Rogers 53% to 42%.

Ratings are more cautious. Fox News Power Rankings list Alaska, Iowa, Maine, South Carolina and Texas as toss-ups, with Michigan also a toss-up and Ohio leaning Democratic. Cook Political Report lists Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas as toss-ups. In North Carolina, a final High Point University/YouGov poll had Democrat Roy Cooper 14 points ahead of Republican Michael Whatley.

A Washington Examiner opinion writer argues the map is better for Republicans than polls suggest. The piece cites a New York Times finding that registered white Democrats were 30% likelier to respond to polls than white Republicans, and early-ballot data it reads as favorable in Kansas and South Carolina. The writer is less confident about Ohio and Alaska. CNN ranks the 11 seats most likely to flip.
facts: NYT/Siena: Talarico 50, Paxton 43 in Texas.
NYT/Siena: Jackson 51, Collins 45 in Maine.
NYT/Siena: El-Sayed 53, Rogers 42 in Michigan.
Fox News rates Alaska, Iowa, Maine, South Carolina, Texas and Michigan as toss-ups.
Republicans need 50 seats to keep Senate control.
stories.next: Watch Texas, Maine, Michigan and Ohio as returns arrive tonight.
stories.left: Democrats read the polling as proof that affordability and the war are dragging down Republican incumbents, even in red states. They note that leads in Texas, Ohio and Maine would have looked unthinkable a year ago. Their caution is that poll leads have vanished before on Election Day.
stories.right: Conservative analysts say pollsters have a long record of undercounting Republican voters and that early-ballot data tells a different story. They argue ratings that still show toss-ups prove the race is open. A Republican hold of 50 seats, they say, is plausible even in a bad national environment.
stories.flag: The poll numbers come from search summaries of NYT/Siena and other polls; I did not open the original poll releases.

stories.title: Trump's approval sits near 37% as both parties argue over what the midterms mean
stories.summary: Pew puts approval at 37% and Democrats lead the generic ballot by about 9 points, but both sides dispute what that means.
story: Pew Research puts President Trump's approval at 37%, down from 40% in the fall, according to coverage in the Washington Examiner. On the eve of the vote, Democrats held an average 9-point lead on the generic congressional ballot (Washington Examiner, CNN). The Dispatch argues 2026 could be a bigger blue wave than 2018.

Democrats have their own problem. A Quinnipiac poll found 18% of voters approve of congressional Democrats' job performance, and a Wall Street Journal survey found voters trust congressional Republicans more on the economy, 38% to 32% (Washington Examiner). Sen. Elizabeth Warren says Democrats must be more than the anti-Trump party.

Republican strategists say approval alone will not decide the outcome. One, Dennis Lennox, told the Washington Examiner that credible candidates and turnout operations decide races. Axios reports that Republicans' blame game has started early, and that some Republicans expect to distance themselves from Trump starting Wednesday if they lose. The Dispatch reports GOP voters still cling to Trump despite his numbers.
facts: Pew: Trump approval 37%, down from 40% in the fall.
Democrats lead the generic ballot by an average of 9 points.
Quinnipiac: 18% approve of congressional Democrats.
WSJ: voters trust Republicans more on the economy, 38% to 32%.
Democrats need a net gain of three House seats.
stories.next: Wednesday: whether Republicans distance themselves from Trump after the results.
stories.left: Democrats argue a president under 40% approval cannot protect his party, and that cost of living and the Iran war give voters concrete reasons to punish Republicans. They say a House win would let them investigate and constrain the administration. Their strategists warn that being merely anti-Trump may not be enough.
stories.right: Conservatives say midterm losses are normal for the president's party and that Democrats' favorability is worse than Republicans'. They point out that voters still trust Republicans more on the economy. Several argue that Trump's base turns out for him only when he is on the ballot, which is why he made a final push in red states.
stories.blindspot: Most detailed coverage found came from right-leaning and center outlets; I did not find new left-leaning analysis in these searches.

stories.title: DOJ appeals after judge dismisses its Alaska Senate ballot lawsuit
stories.summary: The Justice Department says it will appeal a ruling that threw out its bid to segregate and investigate Alaska Senate ballots.
story: A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit over the Alaska Senate race, CNN, NPR, Axios and NBC News reported. The suit sought to delay certification and to segregate ballots cast for a second candidate named Dan Sullivan, a name dispute known as "decoy Dan," so voters could be investigated. Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is the incumbent.

The judge dismissed the case on procedural grounds and said segregating ballots for "Daniel J. Sullivan" so law enforcement could investigate voters would violate Alaskans' secret ballot (search summary of coverage). Fox News reports the department is set to appeal, and the case heads to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. The U.S. attorney in Alaska has confirmed parallel civil and criminal investigations.

The Washington Examiner reports DOJ insists it only wants the ballots preserved, not the vote changed. Separately, a federal judge issued an emergency order barring the Justice Department and Homeland Security from demanding that election officials in any state segregate ballots, purge voter rolls or halt ballot processing, according to the summary found.
facts: A federal judge dismissed the DOJ suit on procedural grounds.
DOJ filed a notice of appeal to the 9th Circuit (Fox News).
The U.S. attorney confirmed civil and criminal probes.
The judge said segregating ballots would violate ballot secrecy.
A separate emergency order restricts DOJ and DHS demands on ballots in any state.
stories.next: Watch for a 9th Circuit filing and any dispute over Alaska's certification.
stories.left: Democrats and election-law groups call the suit an attempt to pave the way to contest a Republican loss and to intimidate voters. They say a court order protecting ballots from segregation was needed. They want the Justice Department to stay out of how states count votes.
stories.right: Republicans and the department say preserving ballots is routine and does not change any outcome. They argue that a second candidate with the incumbent's name can confuse voters and deserves investigation. The Washington Examiner reports DOJ describes the suit as an effort to keep evidence, not to delay a result.

stories.title: Californians vote on the Prop 40 billionaire tax, which polls showed trailing and which Props 41 and 42 can cancel
stories.summary: A late PPIC poll had Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no, and either Prop 41 or 42 can erase it even if it passes.
story: California voters are deciding Prop 40, a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state's roughly 200 billionaires, CalMatters and the San Francisco Chronicle report. A late-October PPIC poll found 46% of likely voters in favor and 52% opposed, down from a 52% majority a month earlier (KQED, CalMatters).

The measure survives only if it gets more yes votes than both Props 41 and 42. Prop 41 would bar taxes that get around the state's 1979 spending limit. Prop 42 would ban wealth taxes and retroactive taxes. If either gets more yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 fails (CalMatters). A PPIC analyst said Props 41 and 42 poll better than the tax.

SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West leads the yes side, arguing billionaires should pay for social services. Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who moved out of state, gave $102 million to the committee behind Props 41 and 42, and one report says opponents have spent more than $300 million overall. Gov. Gavin Newsom endorsed Prop 42, arguing a one-time tax would not fix the budget and would drive wealthy residents out. The union said he is "in lock step with his billionaire backers."
facts: Prop 40: one-time 5% tax on net worth above $1 billion.
Late PPIC poll: 46% yes, 52% no (KQED).
Prop 40 fails if Prop 41 or 42 gets more yes votes (CalMatters).
Brin gave $102 million to the committee behind 41 and 42.
Newsom endorsed Prop 42.
stories.next: Results tonight, though close races and late mail ballots can take days to settle.
stories.left: Supporters argue that the ultra-wealthy have gained far more than workers and should fund health care and public services through a one-time levy. They say the countermeasures are designed to trick voters into canceling Prop 40. Labor says Newsom sided with billionaire donors against his own party base.
stories.right: Opponents say a retroactive wealth tax invites an exodus of high earners and a revenue hole from lost income-tax payments. They argue the state would be taxing unrealized value such as stock and art, which is hard to measure. Newsom and other moderates say the budget problem is spending, not a lack of billionaire cash.
stories.flag: Poll figures differ across summaries; the 46/52 split is the late-October PPIC result reported by KQED.

stories.title: Bay Area voters decide a regional transit sales tax BART says it needs to avoid station closures
stories.summary: The measure needs a simple majority, and BART has warned that failure could close up to 15 stations.
story: Bay Area voters are deciding a regional sales tax for transit agencies, the San Francisco Chronicle and KQED report. It would add a half-cent in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties and 1 cent in San Francisco, and it needs only a majority because citizen groups placed it on the ballot (SF Chronicle).

BART has said that if the measure fails, it could close up to 15 stations and run trains every half hour. The Chronicle reported that a transit "death spiral" could double Bay Bridge delays. One pre-election poll had support at 56%, solid but below the 60% cushion backers wanted. A judge ruled the ballot language, which uses the word "preserving," was not misleading (KQED).

Fremont voters also have council races on the ballot, including District 2 (Desrie Campbell versus Keith Parker), District 3 (Kathy Kimberlin versus Vipin Sharma) and an open District 4, according to the Chronicle voter guide. Fremont is served by BART, so a failure would hit local riders.
facts: Half-cent sales tax in four counties, 1 cent in San Francisco.
Passes with a simple majority.
BART warns of up to 15 station closures and half-hour trains if it fails.
One poll showed 56% support.
A judge kept the ballot wording in place.
stories.next: Results tonight; the live count is on SF Chronicle and KQED results pages.
stories.left: Supporters say transit is a public good that cuts traffic and emissions, and a sales tax is the quickest way to prevent service cuts that hit low-income riders hardest. They point to the cost of a transit death spiral in congestion and lost jobs.
stories.right: Critics say agencies should fix costs and ridership before asking for $14 billion more, and that sales taxes fall on lower-income shoppers. They note opponents argued the ballot wording was biased and lost in court. Marc Joffe, spokesperson for the campaign against the measure, is among the critics.
stories.blindspot: Coverage found came from Bay Area center and left-leaning outlets; no right-leaning coverage turned up in searches.

stories.title: U.S. strikes Iran's Qeshm Island as Vance says no deadline for a deal
stories.summary: Officials call the strike defensive after Iran fired at a U.S. aircraft, while Trump and Vance keep talking about a settlement.
story: U.S. forces carried out limited strikes on Qeshm Island late Monday, three U.S. officials told CNN. One official said the strike answered Iranian fire at a U.S. aircraft. The Wall Street Journal reported it first, and The Hill reports the targets were radar detectors and missile launchers. A U.S. official told Fox News it was not the start of further military action.

Vance said the administration has set no deadline for a deal and feels good about a negotiated settlement, while saying Trump retains kinetic options (CNBC). Trump called the conflict a "soft war" and said the U.S. holds the cards (Fox News). He also said the U.S. might have to go after Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected underground nuclear site. Iran says it can reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. meets seven demands, and Mohsen Rezaei called the U.S. response not satisfactory.

Axios reports Vance and Witkoff urge a deal while Netanyahu and Hegseth favor renewed strikes. The war began in late February and has sharply cut traffic through Hormuz. CNN analysis says a Democratic House would hold hearings and could try to limit operations, but major Iran decisions stay with the White House.
facts: Limited U.S. strikes hit Qeshm Island late Monday (CNN).
Targets were radar detectors and missile launchers (The Hill).
Brent was near $105 and WTI near $97 on Tuesday (CNBC).
Iran says it can reopen Hormuz in two days if seven demands are met.
The House passed an Iran war powers resolution 220 to 204; the Senate vote failed 49 to 50.
stories.next: Whether the strikes widen after the election, and any move on Pickaxe Mountain.
stories.left: Critics say the administration is drifting through an open-ended war without congressional authorization, with limited strikes that risk escalation and no end date. They point to higher gas and diesel prices and the war powers votes. They want Congress to restrict operations.
stories.right: Supporters say the strikes are measured and defensive, aimed at the radar and missiles that threaten U.S. aircraft. They argue pressure keeps Iran at the table and that Trump holds leverage while Vance pursues a deal. They note Trump has avoided a full-scale resumption of the war.

stories.title: Russian bombing of an aid site in Zaporizhzhia kills at least 33
stories.summary: CNN reports at least 33 dead with about 50 unaccounted for, while NPR's earlier count was 29 killed and 48 missing.
story: Russian bombs hit a shelter and aid hub in the village of Komyshuvakha in Zaporizhzhia region on Nov. 3. CNN reports at least 33 confirmed dead and about 50 unaccounted for. NPR's earlier report put the toll at 29 killed and 48 missing. Zelensky called it one of the deadliest attacks of the war.

Regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said Russia used KAB-500 and FAB-3000 bombs. Zelensky said the strike came just before a larger attack on energy infrastructure, despite Trump's repeated calls for an energy ceasefire. Local authorities declared three days of mourning.

Zelensky has said Russia, Ukraine and the United States plan technical talks in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said talks would center on security issues that would follow a peace deal.
facts: At least 33 dead and about 50 missing (CNN).
Earlier NPR count: 29 killed, 48 missing.
Weapons included KAB-500 and FAB-3000 bombs (regional governor).
Three days of mourning declared.
U.S.-Russia-Ukraine talks planned in Abu Dhabi in early to mid November.
stories.next: Abu Dhabi technical talks in the first half of November.
stories.left: Critics say the strike shows Russia is escalating while talks are planned, and argue Washington should give Ukraine more air defense and tighten sanctions. They see the energy attacks as a test of whether Trump will back his own ceasefire call.
stories.right: Conservatives split. Some argue the attack proves Moscow cannot be trusted and favor more pressure. Others say the war needs a negotiated end soon and that the United States should not be drawn deeper while its own forces are engaged against Iran.
stories.blindspot: Only two sources found for this story, both center-left; I found no right-leaning coverage of the strike.

stories.title: Oil climbs again on Qeshm strike as the Fed's December hike remains the base case
stories.summary: WTI sits near $97 and the 10-year yield near 4.95%, with traders earlier betting on a December rate hike.
story: Oil rose Tuesday after reports of the U.S. strike on Iran's Qeshm Island, CNBC reported. Brent rose 0.33% to $105.12 a barrel and WTI gained 0.89% to $97.32 at the time of that report. Live market data at 6:32 p.m. Eastern shows WTI at $96.74 and the 10-year Treasury yield at 4.95%.

The Fed raised rates at its September meeting. After a weak September jobs report of 29,000 jobs and a 4.2% unemployment rate, traders cut odds of an October hike (CNBC, Bloomberg). CNBC reported FedWatch odds above 75% for a December hike and Goldman Sachs Asset Management's Lindsay Rosner called one more hike her base case.

Those odds date from early October, and I found no newer reading or coverage of the October Fed decision, so treat them as stale. The Hormuz disruption that began in late February has kept energy prices high.
facts: Brent about $105 and WTI about $97 on Tuesday (CNBC).
WTI $96.74 and 10-year yield 4.95% in live data.
September payrolls rose 29,000; unemployment 4.2% (CNBC).
FedWatch odds of a December hike were above 75% in early October (CNBC).
The Fed hiked in September.
stories.next: The next jobs report and any Fed signal on a December hike.
stories.left: Progressive economists argue that rate hikes on top of a war-driven energy shock punish workers and borrowers, and that fuel prices are a policy choice tied to the Iran conflict. They want relief for households facing higher gas and diesel costs.
stories.right: Conservative economists argue inflation that has run above target for five years justifies further tightening, and that the Fed should stay independent of politics. They blame war-related energy costs on Iran's closure of Hormuz rather than on U.S. policy.
stories.flag: Fed odds come from early October coverage and may be out of date.

stories.title: Apple slides on a weak margin forecast and Palantir drops despite a beat
stories.summary: Apple guided margin to 45% to 46% on memory costs, and Palantir fell on slower contract growth.
story: Apple's first earnings report under CEO John Ternus beat on revenue, but the company guided December-quarter gross margin to 45% to 46%, below the 46.3% analyst average, CNBC reported. CFO Kevan Parekh pointed to higher memory costs and Siri AI costs. Ternus called memory pricing unprecedented and said costs should keep rising beyond December. Live data shows Apple at $331.90, down 1.90%.

CNBC says the September quarter's 47.9% margin included about 1 point from tariff refunds, so without that it would have missed the 47.5% consensus. Most analysts stayed constructive. Evercore ISI kept Outperform with a $380 target and Bernstein kept Outperform at $370, while Barclays stayed underweight.

Palantir fell after third-quarter results as analysts pointed to a slowdown in U.S. commercial total contract value growth (CNBC). U.S. commercial revenue more than doubled to $984 million and topped U.S. government revenue for the first time. Stocks recovered some of their early losses through the day.
facts: Apple guided gross margin to 45%-46% vs 46.3% expected (CNBC).
Apple is $331.90, down 1.90% in live data.
Palantir U.S. commercial revenue rose to $984 million (CNBC).
Barclays stays underweight on Apple.
The S&P 500 rose 0.36% and the Nasdaq 0.83%, while the Dow fell 0.38%.
stories.next: Nvidia reports Nov. 17 after the close; memory-cost commentary will matter for hardware makers.
stories.why: Memory costs are squeezing even Apple's premium margins, and AI software names face high expectations on bookings. For a tech-heavy portfolio, both are signs that AI spending has costs that show up in earnings.
stories.flag: Palantir stock moves vary by source (about 1.65% down at the close in one CNBC report, steeper earlier).

stories.title: India builds a 65-kilowatt ocean thermal plant that also makes drinking water
stories.summary: The Lakshadweep plant uses 1,000-meter-deep seawater to generate power and fresh water, in what IEEE Spectrum calls a step toward commercial viability.
story: India's National Institute of Ocean Technology is building a roughly 65 kilowatt ocean thermal energy conversion plant on Kavaratti in the Lakshadweep islands, IEEE Spectrum and Down To Earth report. It draws cold water from about 1,000 meters deep and runs on the temperature gap with warm surface water.

The plant is designed to make about 100,000 liters of drinking water a day through low-temperature thermal desalination. Down To Earth describes a 3.8 kilometer polyethylene pipeline to reach the deep cold layer. NIOT ran a thermal desalination plant on Kavaratti from 2005.
Sources disagree on temperatures: the deep-water figure ranges from about 5 to 8 degrees Celsius across reports. IEEE Spectrum calls it a small project but a big step toward commercial OTEC.
facts: Capacity is about 60 to 65 kilowatts.
Cold water is drawn from about 1,000 meters.
Target output is about 100,000 liters of fresh water a day.
A 3.8 km HDPE pipeline reaches the deep layer (Down To Earth).
Temperature figures vary by source.
stories.next: Commissioning news from NIOT; I did not find a current construction status.
stories.why: OTEC runs around the clock, unlike solar or wind, so small island grids could use it for base power. The hard part is the large cold-water pipe and low efficiency, which is why a 65 kW plant is a test, not a power plant.
stories.flag: I did not confirm current construction or commissioning status.

stories.title: Neutral-atom quantum computing gets a boost from the Microsoft and Atom Computing machine planned for Denmark
stories.summary: The planned Magne system targets 50 logical qubits built from 1,225 physical neutral-atom qubits.
story: IEEE Spectrum calls 2026 a big leap for neutral-atom quantum computing, highlighting an effort by Microsoft and Atom Computing to deliver an error-corrected machine to a Danish funder. Atoms can be moved around, which makes error-correction schemes possible that static qubits cannot support.

The system, called Magne, was announced in July 2025. Atom Computing supplies hardware, and Microsoft supplies software and error-correction protocols. The target is about 50 logical qubits from 1,225 physical qubits. Denmark's export fund EIFO and the Novo Nordisk Foundation committed €80 million through the QuNorth venture (Data Center Dynamics, Quantum Insider).

Operations were expected around the turn of 2026 to 2027. Logical qubits are error-corrected units, which is why the count of physical qubits needed per logical qubit matters more than raw qubit totals.
facts: Magne targets 50 logical qubits and 1,225 physical qubits.
Atom Computing builds hardware; Microsoft provides error correction.
QuNorth was funded with €80 million by EIFO and the Novo Nordisk Foundation.
Operations were expected around the turn of 2026-27.
Neutral atoms can be repositioned during computation.
stories.next: Whether Magne is delivered and running by the end of 2026.
stories.why: Error correction is the gate to useful quantum computing. A working 50-logical-qubit machine would show whether neutral atoms can scale past lab demos.
stories.flag: Build status in November 2026 is unconfirmed; the specifications come from the July 2025 announcement.

stories.title: NASA's Swift observatory is due to re-enter early Wednesday after a failed rescue
stories.summary: The Space Force predicts re-entry near 12:30 a.m. Pacific Wednesday, with a 1-in-2,100 risk of harm to anyone.
story: NASA says its Swift observatory will re-enter the atmosphere around 3:30 a.m. Eastern on Nov. 4, which is 12:30 a.m. Pacific, with an uncertainty of 11 hours, based on a U.S. Space Force prediction. NASA puts the chance that debris harms anyone on Earth at about 1 in 2,100 (NASA, Space.com).

Most of the spacecraft should burn up. Surviving pieces would land between 20.6 degrees south and 20.6 degrees north latitude. One expert told Space.com the six heavy reaction wheels and some telescope parts, such as lenses and mirrors, are most likely to survive.

A private rescue mission by LINK to boost Swift failed. About three weeks after liftoff it had propulsion and reaction-wheel problems, and NASA announced Aug. 19 that it would no longer attempt the capture. On Oct. 20, Swift went into safe mode because it could no longer compensate for drag.
facts: Predicted re-entry: about 3:30 a.m. Eastern Nov. 4, plus or minus 11 hours.
Risk of harm to anyone: about 1 in 2,100 (NASA).
Debris can fall only between 20.6 degrees south and north.
LINK's rescue mission failed.
Swift entered safe mode Oct. 20.
stories.next: NASA and Space Force will update the prediction; check NASA's Swift blog for confirmation.
stories.why: Swift spent two decades catching gamma-ray bursts, and its loss ends a flagship rapid-response observatory. It also shows how little can be done once an orbit decays.

stories.title: Astronomers propose star collisions as one explanation for JWST's Little Red Dots
stories.summary: Several 2026 model studies argue the puzzling red objects are dense clusters or supermassive stars, not simply black holes.
story: Webb's Little Red Dots are compact red objects in the early universe that astronomers have struggled to classify. A UCLA study, reported in October, proposes that crowded ancient star clusters had frequent stellar collisions, merging stars into huge ones and eventually black holes (ARY News). A UT Austin study from July argues a young globular cluster with a central supermassive star could look almost identical to a Little Red Dot.

A Center for Astrophysics model by Nandal and Loeb found a metal-free star of nearly a million solar masses can reproduce some spectral features, but such a star would stay bright only about 10,000 years, which could explain why the dots seem to vanish.

The black-hole reading has a problem: most Little Red Dots show no X-ray emission and no clear brightness changes. A 2025 Penn State paper proposed a new kind of "black hole star" (Space.com). The field has not settled on one answer.
facts: UCLA: dense clusters with stellar collisions may explain the dots.
UT Austin: a cluster with a supermassive star could mimic a dot.
Nandal and Loeb: a near-million-solar-mass star fits some spectra.
Most dots show no X-rays.
No explanation is confirmed.
stories.next: New Webb observations that test X-ray and variability predictions.
stories.why: If the dots are huge stars or clusters, theories for how early black holes grew so fast may need less exotic ingredients. If they are black holes, the early universe built them faster than models predict.
stories.flag: Findings come from secondary coverage of model-based studies; none is confirmed.

stories.title: Anthropic could begin formal IPO marketing the week of Nov. 9
stories.summary: Bloomberg reports marketing could start as soon as Nov. 9, with trading possibly before Thanksgiving, though dates have slipped before.
story: Anthropic could begin formally marketing its initial public offering as soon as the week of Nov. 9, Bloomberg reported. The Wall Street Journal, cited by CNBC, said it aims to start trading the week of Nov. 16, and prediction markets were split on whether that would happen by Nov. 20.

The company filed publicly with the SEC on Oct. 26 and added financial details in an updated filing a week later. The planned Nasdaq ticker is "ANT." Bloomberg reports the offering is expected to match or beat SpaceX's IPO in size and that Anthropic is seeking up to $3.5 billion from Japanese investors. A Bloomberg headline also says Anthropic revenue is near $17 billion and that it has committed to $895 billion in spending.
The schedule has slipped: Reuters reported in September that launch was at least mid-October. CNBC reports prediction markets see an IPO in 2026 as near certain.
facts: Public S-1 filed Oct. 26; updated filing about a week later.
Planned Nasdaq ticker: ANT.
Marketing could start the week of Nov. 9 (Bloomberg).
Trading could come the week of Nov. 16 (WSJ via CNBC).
Up to $3.5 billion sought from Japanese investors (Bloomberg).
stories.next: Marketing could begin the week of Nov. 9; watch for a price range.
stories.why: A mega-IPO would test investor appetite for AI at a moment when the Nasdaq 100 sits in a correction. It also shows how much capital frontier labs need.
stories.flag: Exact dates differ across reports and are unconfirmed.

stories.title: Nvidia weighs guaranteeing debt for the Nscale data center Anthropic plans to use
stories.summary: Nvidia is in talks to back billions in debt tied to a West Virginia campus where Anthropic would rent about 460 megawatts.
story: Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions of dollars of debt for Nscale's planned West Virginia data center, TechCrunch and Bloomberg reported. Under a residual value guarantee, Nvidia would step in if Nscale defaulted on construction payments, take over the facility temporarily and help find a buyer and tenant.

Anthropic agreed to rent roughly 460 megawatts of compute from Nscale, a deal reported at about $45 billion over six years. Nscale plans to use Nvidia's Vera Rubin chips, and capacity should begin powering Anthropic's services in late 2027 (Bloomberg). Nscale is seeking to go public at a valuation of up to $35 billion, and Nvidia has already agreed to guarantee up to $860 million for a Texas lease.

The deal is not final, and no company has confirmed the terms. The arrangement raises the "circular financing" question Axios flagged earlier, in which a chip supplier props up customers who buy its chips.
facts: About 460 MW of compute for Anthropic over six years.
Reported value: about $45 billion.
Nvidia has guaranteed up to $860 million for a Nscale Texas lease.
Nscale seeks a valuation of up to $35 billion.
Terms are unconfirmed.
stories.next: Whether Nvidia and Nscale finalize the guarantee, and how Nscale's IPO goes.
stories.why: Compute is the bottleneck for AI labs, and chip makers are now putting their own balance sheets behind customers. That helps buildouts happen and adds risk if demand falls short.
stories.flag: Based on anonymous-source reports; no company has announced the terms.

stories.title: Oracle adds Google TPUs, OpenAI's Jalapeño chip and Cerebras to its cloud
stories.summary: It is the first time Google's custom chips will run on another hyperscaler's cloud.
story: Oracle said last week that Oracle Cloud Infrastructure will add Google TPUs, OpenAI's Jalapeño chip and Cerebras hardware, CNBC reported Oct. 27. Analysts say it is the first time customers can use TPUs outside Google's own infrastructure.

Jalapeño is OpenAI's first custom chip, designed with Broadcom and aimed at inference, with initial deployment targeted by the end of 2026 (CNBC, Axios). Oracle's Thiagarajan said Nvidia chips remain "the best, most fungible" and that Oracle is not pivoting away from them. CNBC separately reported that Google is enlisting partners to sell more of its AI chips.

CNBC noted analysts see custom silicon as a growing threat to Nvidia's inference margins. Reports conflict on whether OpenAI will buy TPUs: it said in June it had no plans to, but CNBC confirmed an October report that it is planning to.
facts: Oracle adds Google TPUs, Jalapeño and Cerebras to OCI.
Jalapeño was built with Broadcom, aimed at inference.
Initial Jalapeño deployment targeted by end of 2026.
Cerebras is in an IPO quiet period and did not disclose scale.
Nvidia is up 2.29% today in live data.
stories.next: OpenAI's Jalapeño rollout by year-end and any TPU purchase confirmation.
stories.why: More chip choices on one cloud lowers Nvidia's lock-in and gives buyers pricing leverage. Software portability across chips becomes the next engineering problem.

stories.title: A child dies of measles in New York, the state's first measles death in 30 years
stories.summary: The CDC has sent epidemiologists as U.S. cases pass 4,800, the most since 1991.
story: A child in Lewis County, New York, has died after contracting measles, state and county officials announced Monday. CNN, NBC News and The Hill report it is the state's first measles death in about 30 years. Officials released no further details.

The CDC deployed epidemiologists at the state's request, and its Epi-Aid for New York runs through Nov. 13. New York had 178 cases statewide as of Oct. 24. In Lewis County, 15 cases were reported as of Oct. 14, all among people who had not received the MMR vaccine.
Nationally, the CDC had reported 4,852 measles cases as of Friday, the most since 1991 (CNN). The state health department says it is offering MMR vaccine to any unvaccinated person who asks.
facts: First New York measles death in about 30 years.
New York had 178 cases as of Oct. 24.
Lewis County: 15 cases, all unvaccinated, as of Oct. 14.
U.S. total: 4,852 cases, the most since 1991 (CDC via CNN).
CDC Epi-Aid for New York runs through Nov. 13.
stories.next: Whether more cases are reported in Lewis County before the CDC deployment ends Nov. 13.
stories.why: Measles spreads fast among unvaccinated groups, and deaths show the cost of falling vaccination rates. Outbreaks this size also strain local health departments.
